name: Hiscock's Evaporating Black Hole
description: A black hole that forms and then radiates itself away, built by William Hiscock in 1981 from Vaidya's metric. Inside a surface just outside the apparent horizon negative energy falls in and lowers the mass, and outside it positive energy carries the same mass off to infinity. The event horizon ends after a finite time, and the last point of the singularity is naked.
convention: The mass is the length $m = GM/c^2$ and the null times are lengths, so no factor of $c$ or $G$ stands in a component. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A black hole that glows has to shrink [hawking1974]. Stephen Hawking's calculation of 1974 has it emit particles as a hot body would, at a temperature inversely proportional to its mass, so the hole loses mass, and the less it has the hotter it burns [hawking1974, hawking1975]. He gave it "a finite life of the order of" $10^{71}(M/M_\odot)^3$ seconds, ending in a burst worth "about 1 million 1 Mton hydrogen bombs" ("a fairly small explosion by astronomical standards", he added) [hawking1974]. What does the spacetime of such a hole look like, from its birth to that last flash?¶The trouble is that the radiation's energy curves the very spacetime that radiates it, and Einstein's equations with a quantum field for a source are too hard to solve, even at the first round of an iteration [martindussaud2019]. The way around came in 1981 from William Hiscock, then at Yale and at the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Santa Barbara [hiscock1981]. He built the spacetime of an evaporating hole by hand and then asked what a quantum field does on it, hoping "to learn something of the dynamics" of the real thing "while bypassing the difficulties associated with the back-reaction problem" [hiscock1981]. Paul Davies, Stephen Fulling, and William Unruh had supplied the picture to build from five years earlier: pairs of particles are created outside the horizon, "one of which carries negative energy into the future horizon of the black hole, while the other contributes to the thermal flux at infinity" [davies1976].¶The building material was Prahlad Vaidya's metric for a star that shines, which is Schwarzschild's with the mass a function of a null time [vaidya1951, vaidya1953]. Hiscock's first models use its ingoing form alone: a shell of light collapses and makes the hole, and negative energy then falls in along the ingoing rays and lowers the mass $m(v)$ to zero, with flat space left behind [hiscock1981, guo2023]. The event horizon of such a hole ends after a finite time, at the last point of the singularity, and that point is naked: its light runs out to infinity along a Cauchy horizon [hiscock1981, lubbe2009]. In the second model the radiation also leaves [hiscock1981outgoing]. Inside a timelike surface "near (but outside) the apparent horizon" the metric is the ingoing one, outside it the outgoing one, with positive energy carrying the mass $m(u)$ off to infinity, and the surface itself "may be viewed as a shell of pair-creation events" [hiscock1981outgoing].¶How should the mass run out? Slowly, at the very end [hiscock1981]. Hawking's law carried all the way down has $dM/dv \sim M^{-2}$, a rate of loss that grows without bound as the mass goes to zero [hiscock1981]. Hiscock put a massless scalar field on his spacetimes, cut down to two dimensions by setting $d\theta = d\phi = 0$, and found that unless $dM/dv \to 0$ as $M \to 0$, "an infinite flux of outgoing radiation is produced along the Cauchy horizon" [hiscock1981]. With the outgoing radiation in the model the condition became $dM/du \to 0$, a statement about the retarded time $u$ at infinity and so, he noted, "in principle measurable by a distant observer" [hiscock1981outgoing]. He called it "necessary (but not sufficient)", and the caution was earned: in Yuhji Kuroda's calculation three years later the flux from the naked singularity "can be divergent even when the mass $M$ disappears with the condition" $dM/dv \to 0$ [hiscock1981outgoing, kuroda1984evaporating].¶For a black hole with a regular centre Sean Hayward borrowed the surface of pair creation, "adapting an idea of Hiscock", and thanked James Bardeen "for pointing out the surface layer" that the two joined metrics leave on it [hayward2006]. Christian Lübbe and Paul Tod took it as "a convincing model of the metric for an evaporating black hole" to test Roger Penrose's proposal that initial and final singularities differ in their Weyl curvature, and found that at the singularity's last point "a local conformal extension is possible from the future but not from the past" [lubbe2009]. Eugenio Bianchi, Tommaso De Lorenzo, and Matteo Smerlak followed the entanglement entropy of the radiation on a version with a single pair of shells, where it diverges at the last ray together with Hiscock's flux [bianchi2015]. Pierre Martin-Dussaud and Carlo Rovelli, who call it the Hiscock model, wrote out the maps between its five patches, a job "not fully done in the original paper", and glued a white hole onto its future [martindussaud2019].¶Hiscock next asked the same question of naked singularities with no black hole around them [hiscock1982shell]. With Leslie Williams and Douglas Eardley he studied, the following year, the ones that form where collapsing shells focus, and in every case "the energy flux along the Cauchy horizon diverges in a positive sense" [hiscock1982shell]. They took it as a strong hint that the created particles' back reaction on the metric "will prevent the formation of naked shell-focusing singularities" [hiscock1982shell]. The last moment of a real evaporating hole lies beyond the reach of quantum fields on a given background, which is where Hiscock's calculations live, and is not yet known [martindussaud2019].

related.text: Both halves of the model. Vaidya's ingoing metric with a falling mass shrinks the hole, and his outgoing metric carries the radiation away [hiscock1981outgoing].
The hole between its birth and the start of the evaporation, and the field far away until the first of the radiation passes [lubbe2009].
The space inside the collapsing shell, and the space left once the last of the radiation has gone by [martindussaud2019].

The same pair of streams, negative energy in and positive energy out, around a black hole with a regular centre. Hayward built it by "adapting an idea of Hiscock", and it leaves neither a singularity nor an event horizon [hayward2006].

coordinates.name: Ingoing Vaidya
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of pair creation)}

parameters.description: Mass function of advanced time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$: zero before the hole forms, falling while negative energy flows in, and zero once the hole is gone; $m_0$ is its greatest value in the drawings
Areal radius of the surface where the pairs are created, a length, with $R > 2m$ while the hole evaporates; the outgoing radiation lies beyond it

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ constant along ingoing light rays and $r$ the areal radius. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Vaidya
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of pair creation)}

parameters.description: Mass function of retarded time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$, the mass measured by a distant observer at the retarded time $u$; on the surface of pair creation it equals the mass inside; $m_0$ is its greatest value in the drawings
Areal radius of the surface where the pairs are created, a length, with $R > 2m$ while the hole evaporates; the ingoing negative energy lies inside it

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ constant along outgoing light rays and $r$ the areal radius. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Flat Double Null
coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, \theta, \phi)$, the retarded and advanced times of flat space, with the areal radius $r = (v - u)/2$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
